title: Exactly Eight Wins
statement: In a tournament, each of $12$ players plays each other player exactly once, and every game has a winner and a loser. What is the largest possible number of players who win exactly $8$ games?
hints: Look at the players who do not win exactly $8$ games, and at the games they play against each other.

Count the games by their winners: there are $66$ games in all. If $k$ players win exactly $8$ games each, the other $12 - k$ players play $\binom{12 - k}{2}$ games among themselves, and each of those games is won by one of them.

So $8k + \binom{12 - k}{2} \le 66$. Find the largest $k$ for which this holds. To show that many is possible, let those $k$ players beat every other player and share the games among themselves evenly.
solution:
Each of the $\binom{12}{2} = 66$ games has one winner. Suppose $k$ players win exactly $8$ games each. The other $12 - k$ players play $\binom{12-k}{2}$ games among themselves, each won by one of them, so $8k + \binom{12-k}{2} \le 66$. For $k = 8, 9, 10, 11, 12$ the left side is $70$, $75$, $81$, $88$ and $96$, so $k \le 7$.

Seven players can each win exactly $8$ games. Seat them round a circle and let each beat the next three clockwise, so each wins $3$ of the games among the seven, and let each of the seven beat all of the other five players. Each of the seven then wins $3 + 5 = 8$ games, while each of the other five wins at most $4$. The answer is $7$.
